title: Clear the door first
script: WORKER: If the cabinet catches, this whole passage burns. Shut it off now!
JOHN: Someone is near the pressure door. Clear them first, then cut the pump.
WORKER: We could lose the panel while you wait.
notes: The fire is real; a quick warning prevents a door injury. Links Cassidy A (a person beyond the door) and Prue A (pump and intake are separate).

title: Stop the pump now
script: WORKER: The door will close. Someone could be on the far side.
JOHN: The cabinet is arcing. I am hitting the stop before it catches.
WORKER: We do not even know who is over there!
notes: The immediate electrical hazard justifies stopping. In the alternate sequence it closes the door without checking first. It does not close the transfer intake; see Cassidy A and Prue A.

title: Follow the rising level
script: WORKER: That level sensor has drifted before. If you shut the wrong line, we lose our supply.
PRUE: The pump is off and the level is still rising. Check the flow gauge against the tank.
WORKER: And if the gauge is wrong too?
notes: The independent gauge confirms incoming water. Combine with Prue B (display covers one valve) or Cassidy B (worker sees open transfer) to locate the bypass.

title: Trust the intake display
script: WORKER: The level keeps climbing. It has to be coming from somewhere!
PRUE: The intake on my screen is closed. That gauge drifted before. I am checking the sensor first.
WORKER: If the gauge is right, we are wasting time!
notes: The display is accurate for the Control valve but omits the transfer valve. Sensor inspection is sensible, yet treating the display as proof all intake stopped is wrong. Compare Prue A or Cassidy B.

title: Check the far side
script: WORKER: There is no time to call Loading. That cabinet is smoking!
CASSIDY: Someone answered from Loading. If the pump stop closes that door, they could be trapped.
WORKER: If the cabinet burns, everyone is trapped.
notes: The Loading worker and the electrical danger are real. Connect John A/B (door closes on stop) and Act 2 Cassidy A/B (worker and hatch).

title: Follow the worker’s report
script: WORKER: The screen says closed. Why are you taking the word of somebody behind a flooded hatch?
CASSIDY: They can hear water running through the transfer pipe. I am checking that line.
WORKER: If you go there, who is watching this tank?
notes: The report is a lead, not a complete diagnosis. Combine with Prue A (flow persists) or Act 2 Prue A (the bypass) and independently inspect flow.

title: Equalize the hatch
script: WORKER: The water is rising around her! Open the hatch!
JOHN: The pressure marker is red. I am equalizing it before we force anything.
WORKER: If that takes too long, she drowns!
notes: The marker shows unequal pressure; equalizing prevents a surge, but rescue is urgent. Pair Cassidy A (worker location and valve sound) with John B (consequences of opening).

title: Force the hatch
script: WORKER: The pressure marker is red. It will flood the passage!
JOHN: She is trapped and the water is rising. Stand back; I am opening it.
WORKER: If you do that, where does the water go?
notes: A fast rescue is a plausible urgent motive. Opening without equalizing sends water toward the passage. Cassidy A or the marker establishes the pressure context.

title: Trace the bypass
script: WORKER: That transfer line is our supply. If you close it, what happens when the tank runs dry?
PRUE: It goes around the valve on the screen. The flow gauge says it is still feeding the tank.
WORKER: You cannot know that without tracing it.
notes: The pipe labels and local flow reading confirm the bypass. Combine Act 1 Prue A (rising level) with Cassidy B (worker identifies transfer valve).

title: Keep supply flowing
script: WORKER: That transfer valve is feeding the tank. We need it closed!
PRUE: The Control valve is closed and we need water for the crew. I am leaving the transfer open until we confirm it.
WORKER: The tank may not last that long.
notes: Maintaining water is reasonable. The open transfer is an independent gravity feed and keeps filling the tank. Compare Prue A, Cassidy B, and local flow markers.

title: Ask through the hatch
script: WORKER: She needs help now. Stop talking and open the door!
CASSIDY: She says water is against the hatch. I need her position before we move it.
WORKER: Her position will not matter if she drowns!
notes: Direct testimony gives water side and person location. Connect to John A/B on the hatch and Cassidy B on the nearby valve. Other sources remain accessible.

title: Take the valve report
script: WORKER: You cannot send her back for a valve. She is injured!
CASSIDY: She says the open transfer valve is beside the Loading pipe. We can close it ourselves.
WORKER: Then who is getting her out?
notes: The worker’s report identifies the location but does not demand she operate it. Combine Prue A (bypass path) and Act 1 Prue A (tank rising); coordinate rescue or do one after the other.

title: Move around the line
script: WORKER: Leave the analyzer. You cannot get it past that bracket!
JOHN: I will brace it and move the unit around. Keep everyone away from that pipe.
WORKER: If that line lets go, you will be right beside it!
notes: The analyzer is obstructed by a damaged line. Combine Cassidy A/B (it is a pressurized relief line) and Prue A (restart can increase pressure). Bracing alone is not proof of isolation.

title: Use powered lift
script: WORKER: Do not restore power until someone checks the pump controller!
JOHN: The manual lift is slow, and the analyzer is blocking the passage. We need the powered lift.
WORKER: That circuit may start more than the lift!
notes: The lift is useful but restoring its circuit can trigger the armed local restart. Compare Prue A/B. The manual crank, safe isolation, or another method can work.

title: Check the local restart
script: WORKER: Leave the power alone! Without it we cannot lift the analyzer.
PRUE: The schedule is canceled at Control, but this local controller is still armed. I am isolating the restart.
WORKER: Are you sure that will not shut the doors too?
notes: The local controller and diagram confirm an independent restart. Combine John B (power restored for lift) and Cassidy A (pressure-line condition) to understand the consequence.

title: Restore the circuit
script: WORKER: The pump controller still has a light on. Do not reset that circuit!
PRUE: I canceled the schedule at Control. We need power to clear the analyzer; I am resetting it.
WORKER: What if that light is a separate restart?
notes: Control timer cancellation does not disable local restart; verify on the controller. Compare Prue A and John B. It is understandable to seek lift power.

title: Identify the damaged line
script: WORKER: If we do not open the relief valve, the pressure stays in the tank!
CASSIDY: That is the split relief line beside the analyzer. Check whether it is isolated before anyone moves it.
WORKER: And if there is no other way to relieve it?
notes: The split line beside the analyzer is the relief line. Pair with John A (physical obstruction) and Prue A (restart can add pressure). Check isolation using gauge and valve position; do not assume a zero reading alone proves safety.

title: Open the relief valve
script: WORKER: That line is split. Opening it could flood the escape route!
CASSIDY: The tank is still under pressure, and the analyzer is in our way. I am cracking the relief valve.
WORKER: How can you know the pipe will hold?
notes: Pressure needs handling; a split relief line makes opening risky. Pair John A (obstructing line), Cassidy A (inspect/isolate), and the local gauge. Use separate outlet, repair or hold if sound.
